rv.q: This spin on the Molière classic only really comes to life when Mark Rylance takes the stage.
Altogether, a remixed mixed-bag.
The result is patchy, but at times uproarious.

Rylance, often playing directly to the audience, has enjoyable moments of excruciating Father-dancing at the wedding and, as the English farce tradition demands, is more than once reduced to his white Y-fronts and vest.
Bold, hilarious and heartfelt, Tartuffe (Remixed) reimagines Molière's timeless comedy through the lens of a contemporary Nigerian–Jamaican family.
Tartuffe (Remixed) is as farcical as farce can be, overflowing with outrageous humour and joyful jesting that has the audience laughing uproariously.
As a show, it’s as big of heart as it’s loud of mouth and, ultimately, just an awful lot of fun.
Overall then, a refresh which speaks to multiculturalism, loyalty, traditions, and in a world which daily gives us cause to question established truth, a healthy and appropriate dose of cynicism.
The Nigerian-Jamaican setting suits Molière nicely, and Raymond’s production will only grow in strength as the run continues.
While the project is flawed, she and Rylance make this worth seeing.
While overall this is an uneven production – a bit of a curate’s egg you might say – a cornucopia of energetic performances keeps the action simmering.
This is a witty and impressive adaptation of the classic comedy that gives new life to a story centuries old.
This new version blasts the cobwebs from Moli re's wig and electrifies the original narrative with new relevance.
Tartuffe (Remixed) is energetic, clever and hilarious, while still finding room to explore family, faith and tradition.
Raymond’s experience adapting 15 Shakespeare plays and deftness in verse pulses through effortlessly: one of the production’s greatest strengths.
It is a masterclass in comedic performance and characterisation as he, at first, subtly tries to bend everything to his will but becomes bolder as he succeeds.
The whole production feels full of colour, movement and personality.
This is a group effort but it’s impossible not to come back to the unctuous figure of Rylance.
A riotous night out is to be had here, whether you know the original text or not.
This is an evening of powerful, enriching theatre that restores one’s faith in humanity.
It’s an energetic, inventive and thoroughly entertaining night at the theatre.
This is definitely a highlight, and well worth going to see if you can get your hands on tickets.
Mark Rylance is the major drawcard in this production, and he is very entertaining as the ingratiating vicar whose true colours begin to be revealed, especially in the second half of the play.
The show is definitely worth the watch, at a young, independent theatre that isn’t afraid to tackle some difficult themes.

cn.t: Critics praise Raymond's energetic Nigerian-Jamaican adaptation and Rylance's scene-stealing performance as the conman pastor, though some find the rhyming couplets take adjustment and question whether the update loses political bite.
